subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Verify Rolle's theorem for the function f(x) = x² + 4 in [−3, 3].

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what you check first, and how you reach the value of c.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Check the three conditions on [−3, 3]
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both end values come to 13. Show the arithmetic — 'f(−3) = f(3)' asserted without the two numbers does not earn the condition.
steps.memory_tip: x² + 4 gives the same value at x and at −x, so a symmetric interval must have equal end values. Checking it is still part of the answer.
lines: f(x) = x² + 4 is a polynomial function, so
(i) f is continuous on the closed interval [−3, 3]
(ii) f is differentiable on the open interval (−3, 3)
∴ f(−3) = f(3), so all three conditions of Rolle's theorem hold on [−3, 3].

recall.must_convey: That f is a polynomial, so continuous on [−3, 3] and differentiable on (−3, 3), and that f(−3) = f(3) = 13.
accept: it is a polynomial so it is continuous and differentiable, and both ends give thirteen
f of minus three is thirteen and f of three is thirteen
check continuity, differentiability and the equal end values first
polynomial kabatti continuous, rendu ends thirteen vasthundi
nine plus four is thirteen at both ends

steps.why: This mark is for the three conditions, taken together. A value of c written down without them answers a different question — Rolle's theorem gives a c only when all three conditions hold.
common_mistakes: Squaring −3 as −9, which makes f(−3) = −5 and the third condition fail.
Writing 'f is continuous and differentiable' without naming the closed interval for one and the open interval for the other.

steps.label: Find c from f′(c) = 0
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The constant 4 differentiates to 0, so only 2x is left. Say in words that c = 0 lies inside the interval.
steps.memory_tip: The lowest point of x² + 4 is at x = 0, and the tangent at the lowest point of a parabola is horizontal.
lines: By Rolle's theorem there is a c ∈ (−3, 3) with f′(c) = 0
−3 < 0 < 3, so c = 0 lies in the open interval (−3, 3)

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified, with c = 0 ∈ (−3, 3)

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = 2x, so f′(c) = 0 gives c = 0, and that 0 lies inside (−3, 3).
accept: differentiate to get two x, set it to zero, so c is zero
c equals zero and zero is between minus three and three
two c equals zero so c is zero, which is inside the interval
derivative two x zero pettina c zero vasthundi
the answer is c equal to zero

steps.why: The root of f′ has to be tested against the open interval before it can be quoted. Here 0 is inside (−3, 3), so the theorem is verified; a root outside the interval would have to be rejected.
common_mistakes: Differentiating x² + 4 as 2x + 4, by carrying the constant through instead of differentiating it to 0.
Stopping at c = 0 without saying that 0 lies in (−3, 3).

insider_note: f(−3) = f(3) = 13, so condition (iii) holds even though neither value is zero — Rolle does not require the endpoints to be zero. c = 0 follows at once.
